routes.description: Establish that universally binding moral truths require a nonhuman objective standard, identify that standard with God's immutable and revealed character, and show that secular welfare, preference, convention, and contract accounts cannot supply equivalent moral objectivity or obligation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if objective moral absolutes are established, God's necessary character is shown to ground both their truth and authority, and the proposed secular standards are shown unable to explain their universality, nonarbitrariness, or prescriptive force.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective moral truth and obligation require God's character as their necessary, nonhuman foundation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that at least some actions possess universally true moral status independent of individual or collective preference.
Explain how God's immutable character, rather than an arbitrary divine choice, constitutes the objective moral standard.
Show why consequence, preference, convention, and contractual agreement cannot generate universally binding moral duties.
Connect God's nature, creative authority, and purposes to prescriptions that bind human agents.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how revelation and divine omniscience provide access to moral requirements and informed guidance about their application.
Use difficult cases to test whether harm-oriented secular standards preserve the moral judgments they purport to explain.

routes.description: Reject the claimed necessity of a divine foundation by distinguishing definitions from objectively assessable judgments, grounding moral inquiry in real consequences, intentions, and impartial rule construction, and showing that divine-nature claims do not independently explain goodness or obligation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a coherent secular method can yield objective assessments or justified rules without God, or if the divine account fails to establish moral absolutes, nonarbitrary goodness, or a valid transition from facts about God to binding duties.

motionBridge.description: Show that God is not required for defensible moral truth or obligation because secular inquiry is viable or divine grounding is explanatorily incomplete.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish the selection of a moral standard from the objective truth of judgments concerning suffering, consequences, intentions, and circumstances.
Explain how welfare-sensitive reasoning and impartial contractual construction can justify rules without presupposing divine existence.
Test whether identifying goodness with God's nature makes the divine standard circular, arbitrary, or modally unexplained.
Require an account of how descriptions of God's nature, power, creation, or judgment entail reasons or duties to obey.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish God's possible role as an omniscient source of information from the facts that make conduct morally right or wrong.
Separate the existence or justification of moral requirements from motivation, compliance, punishment, and practical deterrence.

sections.title: Moral Objectivity and the Existence of Absolutes
sections.rationale: Defines the phenomenon requiring explanation and tests whether morality involves intrinsic universal truths, objectively assessable claims under a chosen standard, or context-sensitive judgments about consequences and intentions.

sections.title: Divine Nature, Necessity, and Nonarbitrariness
sections.rationale: Addresses whether God's immutable character supplies a necessary moral standard or leaves unresolved circularity, contrary-nature possibilities, and the basis for calling the divine character good.

sections.title: Secular Welfare and Impartial Rule Construction
sections.rationale: Examines whether facts about suffering, potential conscious states, social consequences, and veil-of-ignorance reasoning can support objective assessments or justified rules without God.

sections.title: Moral Obligation and the Is-Ought Bridge
sections.rationale: Tests how either foundation produces binding prescriptions, with particular attention to whether creation, ownership, divine purposes, definitions, or secular commitments provide reasons agents ought to act.

sections.title: Omniscience, Revelation, and Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: Distinguishes the metaphysical ground of morality from access to relevant facts and evaluates whether omniscience and revelation establish foundation, reliable guidance, or only informational authority.

sections.title: Counterexamples, Motivation, and Practical Force
sections.rationale: Organizes the disputed cases involving hidden harm, rule consequences, disobedience, punishment, and deterrence to test each account without conflating moral truth with motivation or compliance.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Moral truth requires a mind-grounded, nonarbitrary source, while an atheistic appeal to consequences cannot impose universally binding moral values.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening argument is delivered by Matt after Scott explicitly asks him to present his case from the ground up.

response.rationale: Constructively argues that universal moral truth needs a nonarbitrary mind-grounded source and denies that consequences alone supply universality.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: A clear constructive statement, though its necessity premise is asserted more than demonstrated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is recoverable, but 'mind-grounded,' 'nonarbitrary,' and the scope of atheistic accounts need further specification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The excerpt advances necessity while offering mainly a challenge to the alternative, not an exhaustive warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move leaves the decisive bridge from universal bindingness to a mind, and then to God, substantially unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Its central necessity claim rests largely on an expressed inability to see secular justification rather than representative support or alternative comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level claim that objective morality requires a divine-type foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: No sufficiently developed alternative is assessed in this opening span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how a welfare assignment acquires universal truth value and says an atheistic worldview lacks justification for universality.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: Secular moral inquiry can adopt the substantive aim of promoting flourishing and reducing unnecessary suffering while recognizing that the definition of morality is not itself a truth claim.
moves.attributionBasis: Scott takes the floor after Matt yields and explicitly contrasts top-down and bottom-up approaches while explaining his own practical moral concern.

components.text: Contacts the demand for a secular moral standard by identifying flourishing and unnecessary suffering as the substantive objects of inquiry.
Does not yet establish why the adopted welfare aim is universally binding rather than selected.

response.rationale: It distinguishes arbitrary word definitions from substantive inquiry but only partially answers the universality challenge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive topic is contacted, while the binding-force component remains unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes definitional choice from the adopted substantive aim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It modestly states what secular inquiry can investigate without yet claiming a complete foundation.

charity.alternative: The pro challenge concerns the truth or authority of the welfare standard, not merely the arbitrary meaning of the word morality.
charity.decisiveQualification: Selecting welfare as the subject of inquiry does not alone establish universal obligation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The definition-versus-substantive-aim distinction is coherent, with a bounded missing bridge to normativity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is supported by an intelligible account, but the welfare standard itself is not independently defended here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally advances the secular-objectivity route without completing its normative bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly recognizes the concern about assigning value, though it does not fully answer it.

moves.evidenceBasis: Clifton calls words arbitrarily definable and then identifies maximizing flourishing and minimizing unnecessary suffering as his actual concern.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Morality is grounded in God's immutable nature and essence rather than arbitrary commands, and that enduring standard is disclosed through divine self-revelation.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt expressly rejects the divine-command formulation attributed to him and states the character-based Christian account during the ensuing exchange.

components.text: Offers God's nature and essence as a nonarbitrary moral standard in place of a merely selected definition.
Does not directly show why a character-based standard defeats the secular distinction between choosing a standard and objectively applying it.

response.rationale: The reply supplies the proposed divine standard but only partly addresses the secular account's structure.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the foundational issue but leaves the opponent's central definitional distinction largely intact.

precisionFindings.rationale: The character account is clear, but 'standard' and the relation between nature, goodness, and revelation remain compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The identification of God with the standard is stated confidently without resolving the stated Euthyphro-style question.

charity.alternative: A divine-nature version of the dilemma asks whether God's nature is good independently or goodness simply means conformity to that nature.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling God the standard does not by itself dissolve that explanatory challenge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A coherent third formulation is stated, but the inference from immutable nature to nonarbitrary goodness remains materially incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The account relies primarily on theological assertion and revelation rather than a defended warrant for moral status.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the central divine-nature bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply acknowledges the nature-based dilemma but answers it largely by restating the disputed standard.

moves.evidenceBasis: Slick rejects command theory, identifies morality with God's nature and essence, and concludes that God is the standard.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: God's fixed identity does not explain why an eternally contrary divine nature is impossible, leaving the alleged necessity and nonarbitrariness of the divine moral standard unexplained.
moves.attributionBasis: Scott repeatedly advances and refines the possible-world and hypothetical-world challenge, with Matt's short answers serving as the objects of that sustained examination.

components.text: Directly challenges whether immutability explains why God has this moral nature rather than a contrary eternal nature.

response.rationale: The reply squarely tests the claimed necessity and nonarbitrariness of the divine standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive modal-explanatory premise.

precisionFindings.rationale: The counterfactual and its limited target—the unexplained necessity claim—are clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asks for an explanation rather than claiming that the contrary nature is actual.

charity.alternative: God's nature may be essential and therefore identical across every world in which God exists.
charity.decisiveQualification: Essentiality describes modal invariance but still requires an account of why that nature is morally authoritative or nonarbitrary.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between fixed identity and explanation of the fixed properties is coherent and directly pressures the inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The modal challenge is well supported by the exchange, with only the deeper modal framework left implicit.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the central divine-nature bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection preserves the essential-nature response while identifying the remaining explanatory demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span presses whether there is a reason God has the nature he has and contrasts that question with the claim that God simply cannot be otherwise.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: A hypothetical that reverses God's essential holy and righteous character cannot test divine morality because it replaces the theological subject whose nature grounds the standard.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt directly answers the proposed alternate divine nature, explains why he will not grant it, and concludes by restating his revealed-character account.

components.text: Rejects the contrary-nature hypothetical on the ground that changing God's essential holiness changes the subject.
Does not explain why the actual essential nature is good or uniquely possible.

response.rationale: It addresses the modal hypothetical but not the objection's remaining evaluative demand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive counterfactual is contacted, but only one component of the explanatory challenge is answered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The essential-identity claim is clear, although labeling the scenario idolatrous blurs logical, theological, and evaluative objections.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Essential identity can block a same-God counterfactual, but it does not fully defeat nearby possible-standard challenges.

charity.alternative: The hypothetical need not claim that the contrary being is numerically the Christian God; it can test whether nature-based moral authority is explanatory rather than stipulative.
charity.decisiveQualification: Changing the subject answers identity but not the comparative standard question.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The essential-property response is coherent but leaves a material scope gap between numerical identity and moral explanation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The response asserts revealed holiness and righteousness without independently supporting the claimed modal restriction.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the divine-circularity challenge, though incompletely.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response narrows the hypothetical to identity and thereby omits its strongest explanatory interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Slick calls the scenario idolatrous, distinguishes changing truth conditions from redefining God's character, and restates God's holiness and revelation.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: If God is the sole standard by which God is evaluated, believers lack a noncircular basis for determining that the divine standard is good rather than profoundly harmful.
moves.attributionBasis: Scott clarifies the counterfactual, tests dishonesty for logical impossibility, and then explicitly states the circular-standard objection as the conclusion of his questioning.

components.text: Directly argues that identifying God as the sole standard makes the evaluation of God's goodness circular.
Explains that refusing the counterfactual does not supply an independent basis for evaluating the standard.

response.rationale: The move consolidates the modal exchange into a direct circularity objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly reaches the decisive nonarbitrariness inference and its practical epistemic consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alleged circularity and the missing independent evaluative standard are stated clearly.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is proportionate to the self-standard formulation presented in the exchange.

charity.alternative: A foundational standard may be self-authenticating and need not be assessed by a higher moral standard.
charity.decisiveQualification: That foundational stopping point still needs to explain why conformity supplies moral rather than merely definitional authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from sole self-evaluation to lack of independent moral assessment is strong, with a bounded foundationalist response remaining.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The challenge is grounded in the opponent's stated identification of God with the standard and develops its consequence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central divine-circularity bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly targets explanatory circularity without assuming every foundation needs a higher foundation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Clifton says the view provides no standard for judging God good other than God himself and draws the resulting epistemic concern.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: A divine-nature account supplies no rational reason to obey God when its justification that God is good reduces to the circular claim that God conforms to God's own nature.
moves.attributionBasis: Scott supplies the extended practical example and carries it through the successive questions about wrongness, divine nature, goodness, and reasons for compliance.

components.text: Challenges the move from conformity to God's nature to a rational reason for human obedience.
Uses the absence of an external evaluation to argue that the practical authority claim remains unsupported.

response.rationale: The reply translates the circularity concern into the distinct is-ought and reasons-for-action problem.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the missing normative-authority bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reasons-for-obedience demand is clear, though 'rational assessment' and rejection of God mix moral authority with broader belief or allegiance.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The argument supports absence of the stated moral reason more strongly than the broader conclusion that rational people should reject God.

charity.alternative: God's status as creator, perfect being, or ultimate end might provide reasons beyond the bare definition of goodness.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those reasons were not supplied by the nature-is-good circular formulation targeted here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The normative-gap objection is strong, though its final broad practical conclusion exceeds the narrower premises.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dialogue supports the circularity diagnosis, but alternatives such as creative authority are not yet compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the con is-ought bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly attacks the presented account but briefly overextends to rejection of God generally.

moves.evidenceBasis: Clifton says conformity to God's own nature leaves him without a rational basis for assessing that being as a good moral foundation or obeying it.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: God knows all actual and potential facts, so divine moral revelations may rest on relevant reasons that limited human agents cannot fully understand.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt responds immediately to Scott's practical objection and explicitly invokes divine omniscience to distinguish God from an ordinary human adviser.

components.text: Offers divine omniscience as a reason to trust that revelations rest on considerations unavailable to limited agents.
Does not explain why superior information makes the revealer morally good or authoritative.

response.rationale: It answers the epistemic trust question more than the foundational circularity or obligation question.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: A secondary informational component is contacted, while the decisive normative component remains unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The epistemic claim is clear and qualified by 'may not understand,' but the range of revelations and reasons is broad.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Omniscience supports possession of relevant facts, but not by itself the benevolence or authority of the disclosed prescription.

charity.alternative: The objection grants divine knowledge but asks why knowledge or self-conformity generates a duty to obey.
charity.decisiveQualification: Epistemic superiority is not yet normative authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The trust inference has force if divine goodness is assumed, but that assumption is precisely under challenge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Omniscience is definitionally invoked, while the reliability and moral relevance of revelation remain assumed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the subsidiary revelation-and-omniscience bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply substitutes an informational answer for much of the opponent's practical-reason demand.

moves.evidenceBasis: Slick contrasts an omniscient God with an ordinary adviser and says revelations can have reasons humans do not understand.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Because God knows every end result, divine omniscience permits perfect moral judgments and informed prescriptions about which actions agents should and should not perform.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly answers Clifton's question about omniscience and consistently presents Slick's divine-knowledge argument.

components.text: Argues that complete consequence knowledge enables informed prescriptions and thus supplies an epistemic reason for deference.
Does not establish that consequences or knowledge make God the ontological moral standard.

response.rationale: The answer develops informational competence but leaves foundation and binding authority separate.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts practical epistemic reliability, not the decisive circular-goodness component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference is clear, but 'perfect judgments' ranges from factual forecasting to moral correctness without an explicit bridge.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Knowing all outcomes does not alone establish a value function or perfect moral judgment.

charity.alternative: Omniscience can make God the best-informed adviser while consequences remain what determine rightness.
charity.decisiveQualification: Perfect information and moral grounding are distinct roles.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from complete outcome knowledge to factual competence is sound, but the step to perfect moral judgment assumes the disputed standard.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claim depends on asserted omniscience and an unstated evaluative rule.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly contacts the subsidiary epistemic bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not adequately address this strongest intermediary interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: Slick argues that knowing every end result lets God reveal what agents should do and make perfect judgments.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: If consequences determine which actions are right, omniscience makes God an informational intermediary who communicates those facts rather than the foundation that makes the actions right.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly develops a hypothetical theistic concession and draws the intermediary-versus-standard distinction in his own turn.

components.text: Identifies that complete knowledge explains reliable transmission of consequence facts, not what makes an action right, and states the intermediary consequence.
Concedes that limited humans might rationally defer to an omniscient source for information.

response.rationale: The reply expressly distinguishes epistemic access from the metaphysical foundation asserted by the pro case.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly diagnoses the equivocation between informed adviser and moral standard.

precisionFindings.rationale: The intermediary-versus-ground distinction is sharply stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Under the pro move's consequence-based explanation, the limited conclusion follows.

charity.alternative: God's nature, rather than consequences, might ultimately determine rightness while omniscience only guides application.
charity.decisiveQualification: The targeted argument specifically appealed to end results to explain perfect judgments.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The ground/access distinction directly defeats the inference from omniscience to ontological foundation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant is anchored in the opponent's own appeal to consequences, with the broader divine-nature alternative properly separable.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary information-versus-foundation bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply carefully conditions its critique on the consequence-based scenario actually offered.

moves.evidenceBasis: Clifton grants deference to an omniscient being but argues this makes God a middleman communicating the consequence facts that do the moral work.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: As with conventional measurement standards, a moral definition may be selected by humans while particular judgments assessed against that standard remain objectively true or false.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton introduces and develops the ruler analogy immediately after Slick's objection to subjective standards.

components.text: Directly answers the truth-value challenge by distinguishing selection of a standard from objective truth under that standard.
Shows that objective evaluation need not require a divine evaluator, though it does not establish categorical obligation.

response.rationale: The ruler analogy directly develops the secular conception of objective application.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts objectivity, with the universal-bindingness component still incomplete.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional sense of objective truth is stated plainly.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is limited to objectivity relative to a selected standard, which the analogy supports.

charity.alternative: The pro demand is for categorically binding moral truth, not merely accurate measurement under a convention.
charity.decisiveQualification: Objective application under a chosen standard does not alone establish objective selection or obligation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy soundly distinguishes conventional standards from objective application, subject to the explicit limitation on categorical normativity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The measurement analogy gives concrete conceptual support, though moral and metrological standards may differ in authority.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central secular-objectivity bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly illuminates one ambiguity in objectivity while leaving the stronger pro demand visible.

moves.evidenceBasis: Clifton uses the foot and ruler analogy to argue that a selected standard permits objectively true or false applications.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Given moral absolutes that require an objective standard, the failure of atheistic systems to justify such a standard leaves the theistic account validated by impossibility to the contrary.
moves.attributionBasis: Slick identifies his eliminative argumentative form and explicitly contrasts atheistic and theistic justification of moral absolutes.

components.text: Rejects the chosen-standard account as unable to justify moral absolutes and invokes an eliminative theistic alternative.
Challenges whether secular welfare can account for universal moral truth.
Does not answer the circularity objection to the remaining theistic option.

response.rationale: It contacts secular insufficiency but assumes both a two-option field and the success of the theistic alternative.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The main secular challenge is contacted, while rival possibilities and internal theistic objections remain unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is clear, but 'only two options,' 'atheistic systems,' and 'moral absolutes' are not adequately bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Negating one member validates another only after an exhaustive dichotomy, which is not established.

charity.alternative: Secular realism, constructivism, contractualism, and conditional objectivity represent importantly different alternatives.
charity.decisiveQualification: The stated two-option elimination does not show that these collapse into one defeated alternative.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abstract disjunctive form is valid, but the crucial exhaustive dichotomy and negation of the secular side are unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Both the existence of absolutes and comprehensive failure of atheistic accounts are asserted rather than established in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It expressly claims motion-level validation of the necessary theistic foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move materially compresses the alternative space into an undefended dichotomy.

moves.evidenceBasis: Slick states that with two options negating one validates the other, asserts moral absolutes, and challenges atheistic accounting.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Torturing babies to death merely for pleasure is wrong for everyone, and God's revealed prohibition on murder supplies the standard supporting that universal judgment.
moves.attributionBasis: Slick defines moral absolutes, supplies the torture example, and expressly grounds its truth in divine revelation.

components.text: Offers a purported universal moral truth and a revealed divine standard as more than objective application under convention.
Uses an extreme case compatible with welfare reasoning but does not distinguish divine revelation from the secular basis in that case.

response.rationale: The example supports belief in an absolute but does little to establish its uniquely divine ground.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the existence-of-absolutes issue while leaving the comparative-foundation demand largely unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The act, motive, universal scope, and claimed revelatory basis are clearly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The moral judgment is strongly supported as common ground, but the unique grounding inference is not.

charity.alternative: A secular welfare or rights account can also condemn pleasure-motivated torture universally.
charity.decisiveQualification: Agreement on the verdict does not discriminate among foundations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The case coherently illustrates an asserted absolute, but revelation's correspondence with the verdict does not establish revelation as its ground.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The example is specific and compelling for the verdict, while the theological warrant is asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central moral-absolutes bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents the verdict clearly but does not handle the strongest secular explanation of the same case.

moves.evidenceBasis: Slick declares pleasure-motivated torture of babies wrong for everyone and cites God's prohibition on murder as his standard.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: A secret assault on an unconscious person remains wrong even when awareness, pregnancy, disease, discovery, and other stipulated harms are absent, challenging a harm-only moral criterion.
moves.attributionBasis: Slick constructs the coma scenario and expressly applies it as a counterexample to Clifton's stated harm criterion.

components.text: Tests whether a simplified harm criterion can condemn a secret assault when stipulated downstream harms are absent.
Does not show that richer secular standards cannot include autonomy, risk, rule effects, or potential states.

response.rationale: The counterexample contacts a harm-only formulation but not the strongest secular account already available.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It challenges a relevant component while leaving broader secular criteria untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The scenario is clear, but 'no harm' excludes only listed outcomes and leaves autonomy, risk, and rule-level harm unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The case pressures immediate experienced-harm accounts but does not defeat all harm-oriented theories.

charity.alternative: Harm can include violation of autonomy, imposed risk, counterfactual interests, and consequences of permitting the rule.
charity.decisiveQualification: The stipulation of no awareness or discovery does not eliminate these forms of harm.

logicalCoherence.rationale: It is a usable counterexample to a narrow experienced-harm criterion, but its extension to secular welfare generally overreaches.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The concrete thought experiment supports the narrow test, while the 'no harm' premise is underdefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially supports the subsidiary counterexample bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move relies on a materially narrowed version of the opponent's welfare view.

moves.evidenceBasis: Slick stipulates an unconscious victim, no pregnancy, disease, awareness, or discovery, and asks why the assault remains wrong.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: Secular moral reasoning can evaluate actual and potential conscious states together with rule-level social consequences rather than merely maximizing immediate aggregate happiness.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton refines his definition and uses the organ-harvesting thought experiment to explain broader consequences of adopting a rule.

components.text: Expands the secular criterion beyond immediate experienced harm to actual and potential conscious states and rule consequences.
Explains how secular reasoning can preserve strongly shared verdicts through broader consequences.

response.rationale: The reply corrects the narrow target and supplies a rule-level mechanism, though the excerpt's organ case does not explicitly revisit every assault stipulation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive narrow-harm assumption and provides a substantive replacement framework.

precisionFindings.rationale: The enlarged criterion is recoverable, but the weighting among actual states, potential states, and rule effects is not specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims a viable evaluative method rather than a completed proof of categorical obligation.

charity.alternative: The hidden-assault case attempts to remove all welfare effects, not merely immediate aggregate happiness.
charity.decisiveQualification: Potential interests and rule-level consequences survive several of the stated stipulations unless expressly excluded.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The richer consequential framework coherently answers simple maximization objections, with weighting and justification still compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The organ-harvesting example concretely motivates rule consequences, though broader empirical and normative support is absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central impartial-rules bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly strengthens the secular view while recognizing what the counterexample tries to establish.

moves.evidenceBasis: Clifton defines the concern in terms of actual and potential conscious states and uses organ harvesting to illustrate consequences of permitting a rule.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: Hypothetical rational construction behind a veil of ignorance can generate impartial rules for social conduct without presupposing the existence or authority of God.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton introduces a named secular approach and fully explains the rational-choice and veil-of-ignorance mechanism across the boundary lookahead.

components.text: Provides an impartial rule-construction method capable of rejecting permission for assault without relying on the victim's later awareness.
Supplies a secular alternative to the asserted two-option elimination.
Offers an impartial procedure that can support universal prohibitions.

response.rationale: The reply presents a secular procedure directly relevant to objective rule justification without divine authority.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the secular-viability demand with an explicit mechanism, though its assumptions are not fully defended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The hypothetical rational-choice procedure and its impartiality condition are clearly described.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that the procedure can generate impartial rules fits the stated mechanism.

charity.alternative: A negotiated contract may express rational agreement without producing stance-independent moral truth or obligations for nonparticipants.
charity.decisiveQualification: The veil supplies impartiality, but the authority and ideal-rationality assumptions still need defense.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The veil mechanism coherently reduces self-serving bias, with one important bridge from hypothetical agreement to binding duty left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The procedure is specifically explained, but ideal rationality and contractual authority are not independently supported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level viability of morality without God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move provides a serious secular construction while leaving its strongest metaethical limitation open.

moves.evidenceBasis: Clifton describes perfectly rational agents negotiating rules behind a veil of ignorance without knowing their social identity.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: A recipient-preference account can assign opposite moral statuses to the same conduct depending on what a recipient wants and therefore cannot furnish an objective standard.
moves.attributionBasis: The alternating dialogue and Slick's explicit second-person criticism clearly attribute this sustained objection to Matt Slick.

components.text: Does not address impartial hypothetical agreement; it substitutes an individual recipient-preference criterion.
Does not engage actual and potential states or rule-level consequences.

response.rationale: The criticism is relevant to crude preference theories but misses the decisive components of the immediately preceding secular accounts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is issue-bearing contrary material without contact with the veil or rule-consequence mechanisms.

precisionFindings.rationale: The example is intelligible, but it shifts from the opponent's multi-factor impartial account to recipient preference alone.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Opposite preferences do not show that an impartial welfare-and-rule account assigns opposite moral statuses.

charity.alternative: The secular view evaluates actual and potential states plus impartial rules, not whether a recipient happens to welcome an act.
charity.decisiveQualification: Consent, autonomy, coercion, and rule consequences distinguish the proposed cases.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference works against simple preference relativism but is a non sequitur against the account actually offered.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The hypothetical supplies vivid illustration but no support for attributing the simplified criterion to the opponent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Despite weak contact with the selected replies, it centrally attacks impartial secular rule construction in intended burden terms.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection materially weakens the developed secular position into a recipient-liking test.

moves.evidenceBasis: Slick claims the same assault changes moral status solely with the recipient's preference and concludes that no objective standard remains.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: A divine moral theory can separate right and wrong entirely from suffering, happiness, and health because a divine nature favoring universal misery would make misery moral by definition.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton introduces the objection as a problem with Slick's worldview and develops the universal-misery hypothetical directly.

components.text: Recasts the contrary-nature hypothetical to expose the consequence of defining morality solely by divine nature.
Shows that the divine account can likewise detach moral status from welfare outcomes.
Challenges whether character identity alone explains goodness.

response.rationale: The counterexample directly tests the claimed nonarbitrariness by varying the stipulated nature and tracking the theory's verdict.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the defining inference and states its troubling consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The in-principle conditional and its target are stated clearly.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stipulated definition of morality by divine nature, the conditional consequence follows.

charity.alternative: A necessarily perfect God could not possess a misery-favoring nature.
charity.decisiveQualification: Invoking necessary perfection must explain goodness independently enough to avoid merely restating the disputed definition.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional counterexample forcefully exposes the theory's detachment from welfare, with the essential-perfection reply remaining available.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument is grounded in the conceded nature-based definition, though its modal premise is hypothetical.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central divine-circularity challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly uses the hypothetical as an explanatory test rather than claiming it is a genuine Christian possibility.

moves.evidenceBasis: Clifton argues that if God's nature favored universal misery, the nature-based definition would classify that misery as moral.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: Even accepting Christianity's factual and moral claims does not by itself supply a motivating reason that compels an agent to obey the divine prescriptions the agent believes are true.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly sets up and repeatedly clarifies a role-playing counterexample in which he accepts every proposition in Slick's worldview.

components.text: Grants the objective prohibition and asks what motivational reason follows for an agent who believes it but intends to violate it.
Grants the Christian factual framework while separating belief in revelation from motivation to comply.

response.rationale: The role-play cleanly separates moral truth and belief from motivation, although motivation is not identical to justification or obligation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the practical-force component and preserves the opponent's premises for the test.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction is clear, though 'reason,' 'motivation,' and what would 'compel' action occasionally run together.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A counterexample agent who believes without complying suffices for the limited non-entailment claim.

charity.alternative: An agent can possess an objective reason or duty while remaining unmotivated or irrational.
charity.decisiveQualification: Failure of motivation does not refute moral truth, but it does refute automatic motivational compulsion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The belief-motivation separation is sound, with some ambiguity between motivating and normative reasons.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stipulated role-play effectively establishes conceptual non-entailment, though it does not settle moral ontology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the subsidiary motivation-versus-ontology bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move repeatedly clarifies that it is testing practical motivation, not denying the believed proposition.

moves.evidenceBasis: Clifton stipulates that he believes Christianity and the complete moral account while still proposing deliberate wrongdoing.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: A Christian may knowingly violate acknowledged moral requirements, but inconsistency between profession and practice does not undermine the existence of objective moral truth.
moves.attributionBasis: Slick introduces the revised scenario, cites his counseling experience, and explicitly distinguishes Christian profession from inconsistent practice.

components.text: Identifies that inconsistent practice does not entail the absence of objective moral truth and states the truth-compliance distinction.
Does not supply the motivating reason the opponent requested.

response.rationale: The diagnostic defeats any ontological inference from noncompliance, but only partially answers the explicit motivation question.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly diagnoses one possible inference while leaving the stated practical demand unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Profession, practice, and objective truth are clearly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that inconsistency does not disprove truth is well matched to the distinction.

charity.alternative: The opponent is testing whether belief supplies motivation, not arguing that disobedience disproves objective morality.
charity.decisiveQualification: The truth-practice distinction is correct but does not resolve that motivational test.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The truth-versus-compliance distinction is logically strong, but it is incomplete as an answer to motivation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction and counseling example support possible inconsistency, though the renewed atheist claim is asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary motivation-ontology conflation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply partly answers a weaker ontological reading of the objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: Slick distinguishes Christian profession from inconsistent practice and says such inconsistency proves nothing about whether objective morality exists.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Christianity can bridge the is-ought gap because its account includes prescriptions, whereas an arbitrary atheistic system cannot derive a binding ought from descriptions alone.
moves.attributionBasis: The wording expressly defends the prior prescription, invokes the Christian worldview, and contrasts it with Clifton's atheistic system in Slick's argumentative voice.

components.text: Claims Christianity contains prescriptions and therefore can state an ought where atheistic descriptions cannot.
Does not explain why the Christian prescription is rationally binding rather than merely asserted.
Does not address whether divine prescriptions could track a harmful stipulated nature.

response.rationale: The reply recognizes the is-ought issue but treats possession of a prescription as completion of the bridge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the central demand while leaving the entailment and authority components unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable, but 'we can' and 'arbitrary atheistic system' conceal the actual bridging premise.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Stating a prescription is not itself a derivation or justification of the prescription.

charity.alternative: The objection asks what makes the prescription binding, not whether Christian discourse contains the word ought.
charity.decisiveQualification: A valid is-ought bridge requires a normative premise or account of reasons.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move conflates asserting an ought with deriving or grounding it and offers no explicit Christian bridging premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The comparative incapacity of atheistic systems and Christian success are both asserted without developed warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally attacks the con is-ought bridge despite weak execution.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply materially weakens the demand into mere availability of prescriptive language.

moves.evidenceBasis: Slick contrasts descriptions with prescriptions, says atheism cannot bridge is to ought, and asserts that Christians can.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: Facts that God created humanity, is powerful, defines morality, or can punish people remain descriptions that do not by themselves explain why anyone ought to obey God.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker introduces a list of Slick's divine claims as examples and explicitly applies Clifton's recurring descriptive-versus-prescriptive objection to them.

components.text: Identifies that listing divine facts and even calling God the standard does not entail a duty, and states the missing-bridge consequence.
Preserves the distinction between truth and compliance while asking for the separate reason to obey.
Treats omnipotence, punishment, and related divine facts as insufficient without a normative premise.

response.rationale: The reply directly isolates the missing normative entailment in the Christian account.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly names the presented premises and the precise conclusion they fail to establish.

precisionFindings.rationale: The descriptions and missing duty conclusion are enumerated with exact scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that these descriptions do not by themselves entail duty is fully calibrated.

charity.alternative: Creation, perfect goodness, rightful authority, or humanity's proper end could combine with normative premises to yield obligation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those bridging premises are not contained in the listed descriptions alone.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move precisely applies the is-ought distinction and avoids claiming that no Christian bridge is possible.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The diagnosis is grounded in a concrete list of the opponent's claims and a clear entailment test.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the pro central normative-authority bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection expressly uses 'by themselves' and thus leaves room for a developed bridge.

moves.evidenceBasis: Clifton lists divine creation, power, moral-standard status, and punishment, then observes that none states why he should obey.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: People ought to do what is right because right conduct is consistent with and glorifies God, the supreme object of worship and the proper moral standard.
moves.attributionBasis: The response explicitly reiterates what Slick says he has already told Clifton and invokes God's glory, worship-worthiness, and status as the moral standard.

components.text: Supplies an explicit proposed reason: right conduct glorifies God, the supreme object of worship and moral standard.
Does not independently explain why glorifying or conforming to God is a reason binding every agent.

response.rationale: The reply states a normative bridge rather than only descriptions, but its key normative premises remain self-certifying.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the demand for a reason but does not defend the reason's authority.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed bridge is clear, while 'greatest object of worship,' 'right standard,' and why glory has normative force are underdefined.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move asserts categorical obligation from divine glory without supporting the normative premise that agents ought to glorify God.

charity.alternative: If God is necessarily perfect, humanity's creator, and its proper end, conformity to God might constitute flourishing or fitting response.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt does not articulate those premises and instead repeats God's supremacy and standardhood.

logicalCoherence.rationale: An explicit reason is finally stated, yet the argument remains circular unless an independent duty to glorify or conform is supplied.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Divine worship-worthiness and the normative force of glory are asserted without defended warrants.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central pro normative-authority bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply offers a real candidate bridge but omits the strongest reasoning that could support it.

moves.evidenceBasis: Slick says people ought to do right because it glorifies God, who is the greatest object of worship and the right standard, and because conduct should conform to him.
